title: Rails queries: indexes, batching, and bounded reports
outcome: Choose SQL work, Ruby work, and batching with attention to memory and business semantics.
useCase: Exports, list screens, and repair jobs.
drawbacks: Batching and snapshot semantics can change the meaning of a report.
cue: Count rows, objects, and queries separately.

trace.title: Scoped relation
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

A report can be correct on ten rows and fail on a million.

Ask how many rows are loaded, how many model objects are built, how many queries run, and whether the order matters.

Use SQL filtering/aggregation when it expresses the required rule. Use pluck for selected values when full model behavior is unnecessary.

Use batches for large iteration, but check the Rails version’s batching order and limits. Rails 4.2 APIs differ from modern cursor options.

An index serves an actual predicate and order. Check the plan on representative synthetic PostgreSQL data.

Avoid assuming an index is used merely because it exists. A large export may need a stable snapshot/job contract rather than paginating a moving live list.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Request scope → SQL predicate/order → database plan → limited rows/batches → Ruby transformation → output. Measure rows, query count, and memory at separate points.

For an export, decide what happens when tickets change while it runs.

A transaction snapshot may give stability but can be expensive over a long job; a materialized export scope is another tradeoff.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
to_a before filtering moves potentially huge work into Ruby memory. Per-row association reads create N+1.

A batch loop that changes its own selection criteria needs a progress rule.
